e.t: Agaritēs; Agaritis is a proper name referring to an Agarite. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 27:31. Because it is a personal designation rather than a common noun, its basic meaning is the identity of the person called an Agarite, not an action, quality, or object. The name’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This adjective describes something or someone as failed or disreputable—shown as unacceptable, lacking approval, or unworthy of trust. It can describe a person, object, or condition that does not meet a sound standard. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Proverbs and Isaiah, so its normal sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The precise force in either passage depends on what the adjective describes.

This adverb means “unveiled” or “in an unveiled manner,” describing something done openly rather than covered or concealed. It tells how an action takes place, focusing on the absence of a covering. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 3 Maccabees 4:6. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the precise force of the word in that passage cannot be described beyond its basic sense: an action or condition presented without a veil.

This Greek LXX noun refers to hearing or to a report—the message or news that is heard and passed on. It can therefore describe what someone hears as well as the spoken account itself. The word occurs 46 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing regular use for heard communication rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage emphasizes the act of hearing or the report received.

Alkimos is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it identifies the same named individual across passages in 1 and 2 Maccabees. The name occurs 15 times, in 15 verses: twelve occurrences are in 1 Maccabees and three are in 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and narrative, but the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

This noun refers to adopting foreign customs—taking on practices associated with peoples outside one's own community. It names the act or pattern itself rather than a person who does it. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. Its central meaning remains broad enough to describe the adoption of outside cultural practices, while the exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This verb means “become dull”: to lose sharpness, clarity, or effectiveness. It describes a change in condition rather than an action performed on something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 27:1. Because the available lexical meaning is brief and no verse text is provided here, the surrounding passage is needed to determine exactly what became dull in that occurrence. Its central idea remains a movement from a sharper or clearer condition to a duller one.

This adjective means “sandy,” describing something connected with or characterized by sand. It identifies the nature or quality of a thing rather than naming an object, person, or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 25:20. Its basic descriptive sense is clear, while the exact force of the adjective in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text.

This Greek LXX verb means “bend back.” It describes an action of curving or turning something backward rather than leaving it straight or forward. As a verb, it expresses what someone or something does. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 11:10; the reference identifies its location, while the basic meaning remains the action of bending back. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “go up,” describing movement toward a higher place or position. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 27:7. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly how that upward movement functions in context, but the basic idea remains movement upward. This word belongs specifically to the Greek translation of the Old Testament and should not be identified with a separate Greek New Testament word merely because English translations may render them similarly.

This word means “axe,” the hand tool used for cutting or chopping wood. It is a noun naming a physical instrument rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, including passages concerning woodcutting, tools, and the image of an axe in relation to the one who uses it. Its exact force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This verb means “die well,” describing the act of meeting death in a good or fitting manner. It is a direct action word rather than a general term for death itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:28. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning is clear: to die well.

This Greek LXX verb means “look off/forward”: to direct one’s sight toward something or someone. It describes an intentional act of looking, rather than merely seeing accidentally. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, across Psalms, Hosea, Malachi, and Song of Songs. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what the person is looking toward and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX adjective means “without want of more.” It describes someone or something that lacks nothing further and is not in need of additional provision. The word focuses on completeness or sufficiency rather than desire, ambition, or spiritual teaching beyond that basic sense. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once each in 1, 2, and 3 Maccabees.

“Unavenged” describes someone or something that has not received vengeance for a wrong. It is an adjective expressing the absence of retribution or redress. In the Greek Septuagint, this word occurs four times, all in Proverbs, so its recorded use is limited to that book within this corpus. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains that a wrong has not been avenged.

This adjective describes something that happens automatically—on its own, without being directly caused or arranged by a person. It can describe an event, action, or result that occurs naturally or spontaneously. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it appears six times, including passages from Leviticus, Joshua, 2 Kings, Job, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is something occurring by itself rather than through deliberate human action.

Achinaan, also rendered Akhinaan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament translation. This name occurs once in the LXX, at Judges 1:10. Because it is a proper name, its meaning here is chiefly identification: it distinguishes one person from others in the passage. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role or significance; the name itself does not provide those details.

Baaz, also rendered Vaaz, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Kings 7:7. Because it functions as a personal or place name in the text, its meaning is primarily its identifying name, not a general concept to be applied elsewhere. The precise person or location identified by the name must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage.

Baithegliō, also rendered Vetheglio, is a proper name identifying a place rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Joshua 18:21. Because the word is a place name and no broader usage is recorded in this corpus, its meaning is chiefly its identification of that named location. The exact significance of the place in Joshua depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Banaia, also rendered Vanea, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies people named in the Greek Old Testament, so its meaning is tied to the individual bearing the name rather than to a general concept. The name occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 12 verses, from Numbers through Ezra. English translations may preserve it as a name, including “Banaia.” The surrounding verse is needed to identify which person is meant in any particular occurrence.

This word is a proper name, identified in English as “Basēza” or “Vasiza.” It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it names a specific individual or designation in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Nehemiah 11:24, so its meaning is chiefly its identifying function rather than a broader concept used throughout Scripture. The exact person or referent must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX adjective means “for marriage,” describing something connected with or intended for marriage. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person or action by itself. In the LXX corpus, it appears once, in 3 Maccabees 4:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense points specifically to marriage and matters associated with it.

Getheremmōn, also rendered Yetheremmon, is a proper name for a specific place. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Joshua 21:24. The available wording identifies the place by name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text here to explain its location, history, or significance. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the name of that place, rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object.

“Tame” means to bring something under control, especially something not naturally submissive or already governed. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person or object: someone or something is being brought into a manageable state. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Daniel 2:40. Its precise force in that passage is best understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “second”: it describes being next after the first or occupying the second position in an order. It is a concise word for rank or sequence rather than a name for a person or object. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Esther, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “spend time”. It describes remaining or passing time in a place or situation, focusing on the activity of staying rather than on a specific action performed. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, including passages in Leviticus, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains spending or passing time.

This verb means “penetrate”—to pass into or through something. It describes movement that goes beyond the surface or enters an area. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 26:28. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains entering or passing through rather than merely approaching or touching. The word is therefore a concrete action term describing something that makes its way inward or across an obstruction.

This Greek LXX noun means an “opinion” or “notion”—an idea, view, or conception held in the mind. It refers to what someone thinks or regards as an understanding, rather than describing an action itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament translation, once in Isaiah 46:13 and once in Lamentations 2:1. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a thought, view, or mental conception.

This adjective describes something that is “difficult of access”—not readily reachable or approachable. It points to limited access rather than simply distance. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 12:21. Its exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here, but its central meaning is a description of something difficult to reach or enter.

This adjective means “having a lot,” describing someone or something that possesses much. It presents abundance or substantial possession as a quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Deuteronomy 4:20. Because the word is an adjective, it functions by describing a person, thing, or situation rather than naming an action. Its exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning is having a lot.

This adjective describes something as genuine and sincere—real rather than false, and marked by honest intention. It can characterize a person, attitude, or quality that is not pretended or deceptive. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this word occurs once, in Wisdom 7:25. That single occurrence supports its basic lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what it describes there. Its central idea is sincerity and truthfulness rather than outward appearance alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “hew in stone; hew”—to cut or shape material, especially stone, by striking or carving it. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, once in Numbers and once in Deuteronomy, so its ordinary sense is focused and specific. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of what was being shaped or cut.

Emioud, also rendered Emiuth, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing mainly in Numbers and once in 2 Samuel. The available information establishes the name and its use as a personal designation, but does not provide enough verse text to explain the identity or role of each person named. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “lawfully” or “legally,” describing an action done according to law or what is legally proper. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 31:25. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is conduct that conforms to law or lawful order.

This word means “outer,” describing something positioned on the outside rather than within or nearer the center. It is an adjective or adverb, so it can describe an outer object, surface, area, or location, or indicate movement or position toward the outside. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 22 times, all in Old Testament verses, especially in Ezekiel’s descriptions of temple areas and structures. Its exact force in any verse depends on what object, boundary, or location it describes.

This Greek LXX noun means “applause”—the approval, commendation, or praise given to someone. It describes favorable recognition rather than a physical object or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 10 times, appearing in both historical books and poetic or wisdom literature. Its central idea remains the positive response shown toward a person or what that person has done. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective means “known,” describing someone or something recognized or familiar. It presents its subject as being known rather than hidden or unidentified. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 18:19. The word’s basic sense remains concise: it identifies something as known. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is recognition or familiarity.

Esdra, also rendered Ezthra, is a proper name referring to Ezra in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies the same person named in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from both Ezra and Nehemiah. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

This adverb means “touching the point; conveniently.” It describes the manner in which something is done or expressed—directly reaching the intended point or fitting the situation well. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 15:38. The available meaning identifies its normal lexical sense, while the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective describes someone or something as “commended” or “commendable”—approved of and worthy of praise. It expresses a favorable assessment, whether it points to a person or to something associated with that person. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 55 times, including 51 Old Testament occurrences and four in the deuterocanonical collection. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains approval or praise.

εὐφυής is an adjective meaning “well-grown” or “shapely,” describing something formed with a pleasing, well-developed shape or appearance. It is a descriptive word rather than an action or title. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Wisdom and once in 2 Maccabees. The precise shade of meaning in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a favorable description of development or form.

Echōchi, also rendered Ekhokhi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:4. Because the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text or a stated definition, its precise referent cannot be described further here. The name itself should therefore be understood as an identifying designation, with its particular reference determined by that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “leaven”: it describes the action of leavening rather than naming leaven as a substance. In these passages, it functions as a verb, expressing what happens when something is leavened. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus and Leviticus. Its central idea is the use or effect of leavening within the sentence where it appears.

This Greek LXX conjunction means “whether.” It introduces an alternative or frames a question involving two possible options, helping connect one thought with another. The word appears once in the Greek text of the deuterocanonical books, at Wisdom 11:18. Its exact force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic function is to present uncertainty or alternatives rather than to name an object, action, or person.

This Greek LXX verb means to watch or look on as a spectator. It describes the act of observing something directly, rather than merely hearing about it. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, across one Old Testament book and several deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is consistent even though the passages differ. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being observed and the surrounding sentence.

Thiras is a proper name, used as the personal designation “Thiras.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in Genesis 10:2 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:5. The available wording gives the name itself rather than an extended descriptive meaning, so it should be understood as a name, not as a common word expressing an action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and genealogy.

This noun refers to a daughter, and it can also mean a village. The surrounding sentence determines which sense is intended. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, with most occurrences in the Old Testament. Its earliest listed occurrence is Genesis 31:50, and its latest is Susanna 1:57. The word therefore commonly identifies a female child or descendant, while in another usage it identifies a village or settlement. It should be understood from the immediate wording and subject of each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to arm someone with a breastplate, that is, to equip a person for protection or battle. It describes the act of making someone ready by providing defensive armor, rather than merely naming the armor itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek text of 1 Maccabees, all within descriptions involving armed forces or warriors. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains equipping someone with breastplate protection.

Ialōn, also rendered Ialon, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in the LXX, in 1 Chronicles 4:17. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its broader family or narrative significance cannot be stated safely. Its basic meaning is therefore the proper name itself: “Ialōn; Ialon.”

Ibaar is a proper name, also rendered Ivaar. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, this name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: 3:6 and 14:5. The available information establishes the name and its alternate rendering, but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning for it. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX noun means “keeper of the wardrobe,” referring to a person responsible for maintaining or overseeing clothing. It functions as a designation for that responsibility, rather than naming the wardrobe itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 22:14, so its normal meaning is clear even though it has limited occurrence. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX adverb means “strongly” or “very much,” intensifying the action or quality described in a sentence. It points to great force, intensity, or degree rather than naming a person, thing, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Deuteronomy, Judges, and Proverbs. Its exact English wording may vary with the sentence, but its central idea remains heightened strength or intensity.

Kaina, also rendered Kena, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its form identifies a named person or place according to the surrounding passage, though the specific referent cannot be determined from the word alone. This name occurs six times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Judges, Isaiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise reference depends on the verse where it appears.

This Greek LXX verb means “seal”: to close, secure, or mark something with a seal. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in Job, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of sealing.

This Greek LXX noun means “accuser”—a person who brings an accusation against someone. It identifies the one making the charge, rather than the person being accused. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus: once in Proverbs and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains the person who accuses another.

This adjective means “hollow; empty.” It describes something lacking what should fill or give it substance, and it can be used of an object, a condition, or a situation. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 73 times, usually expressing the idea of emptiness rather than fullness. Its exact force depends on the noun or situation it describes, but the central picture remains something vacant, without contents, or lacking substance.

Kiradas is a proper name, appearing in the Greek Old Testament as “Kiradas; Kirathas.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Jeremiah 31, at Jeremiah 31:31 and Jeremiah 31:36. Because the available material does not include the surrounding verse text, the precise person, place, or thing identified by the name cannot be stated here.

This Greek LXX noun means a “hollow”—an empty or recessed space within something. It refers to a cavity, depression, or hollowed area rather than to a solid surface. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, including descriptions of physical structures and places. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what object or location is being described.

This word means “hairstyle,” referring to the arrangement or appearance of a person’s hair. It is a noun used for hair as styled or worn, rather than for a person or an action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 10 times, including passages from Leviticus, Numbers, Job, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a person’s hairstyle or hair arrangement.

This word means a scale or scales—the thin covering found on the bodies of certain creatures, especially fish. It is a noun naming that physical feature. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, all within six Old Testament verses, chiefly in passages describing which water creatures may be eaten and which are unclean. The word is also used in a passage involving the rod of Aaron, though the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its precise role there. Its central meaning remains a scale or scales.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Magdan” or “Magthan.” It identifies a particular named place or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition, rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 10:22. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the precise referent cannot be identified further from this word alone.

Makenias is a proper name, used to identify a particular named figure or entity rather than to express a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:21. The available meaning is simply the name “Makenias”; the name itself does not provide a broader descriptive definition. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Maor is a proper name, rendered “Maor,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only once, in Joshua 15:55. The available wording identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain further details about the place or person it names. Its meaning is therefore best represented simply as the proper name Maor within this passage.

This noun means “myth,” referring to a traditional or imaginative story presented as an account. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Sirach 20:19. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be described further. The word’s basic meaning remains a myth or story of that kind, rather than a verb, description of a person, or expression of an action.

Nage, also rendered Naye, is a proper name in the Greek Septuagint. It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs twice in the Septuagint, both times in 1 Chronicles: once at 1 Chronicles 3:7 and once at 1 Chronicles 14:6. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular family or narrative connection cannot be stated here, but its lexical function is that of a personal name.

This Greek LXX noun means “youth,” referring to the stage of life when a person is young. It can describe a person’s youthful years rather than an action or a quality by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 64 times, showing regular use for human youth across many writings. The word appears from Genesis through 4 Maccabees, including passages connected with bodily strength, memory, and the experience of life. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

Noomma is a proper name, identifying a person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 2 Chronicles 12:13. The available information preserves the name itself but does not include the verse text or enough surrounding context to identify whom or what Noomma names. Therefore, its ordinary meaning is its role as a specific name, while its precise referent must be understood from the passage in which it occurs.

This verb means “drunken” or “drunk,” describing a person affected by excessive wine or alcohol. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description of an object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears once, in Deuteronomy 21:20. The word’s basic sense is straightforward: it portrays drunkenness. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical meaning remains centered on being drunk.

gl: for the birds to eat; food for the birds
d: for the birds to eat; food for the birds

e.t: This word refers to something that is food for birds or available for birds to eat. It can function as an adjective describing such a thing, or as a noun naming it. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus represented here: once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains focused on birds as the ones eating the food, while the surrounding verse determines what object or situation is being described.

Olympios is a proper name, referring to a person named Olympios, also rendered Olimpios. It functions as an individual’s name rather than as a description of an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 6:2. The available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so it does not establish additional details about the person or the role he plays in that passage.

“Oudadan; Uthathan” is a proper name, identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The available meaning is limited to the name itself, with these two forms presented as its stated renderings. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 1:9. The surrounding verse text is needed to say more about the person named there. The name itself does not describe that person’s character, role, or significance.

Ochozath is a proper name preserved as “Ochozath” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea, so its ordinary meaning is simply the person’s name. This name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Genesis. The passages where it appears are Genesis 21:22, Genesis 21:32, and Genesis 26:26; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the person’s role in each passage.

This adjective describes something as deeply worthy of pity, sorrow, or mourning—something extremely lamentable. It expresses a strong emotional assessment rather than naming a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject, but the central idea remains that of an especially grievous or pitiful condition.

This verb means to commiserate—to share another person’s sorrow or distress with sympathy. It describes an action of responding compassionately to someone who is suffering, rather than merely noticing the suffering from a distance. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is to express fellow-feeling toward someone in trouble.

“Virginity” refers to the state of a person who has not had sexual relations. This noun names that condition directly, rather than describing a person or an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, with repeated use in Deuteronomy and Judges and additional occurrences in other books. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being discussed.

Pleias is a proper name, also rendered Plias. It identifies a named subject rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs twice, both times in Job: Job 9:9 and Job 38:31. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain its specific reference or significance in either passage.

This word means “launder” or “wash”: it describes cleaning something with water, whether an object, garment, body, or other thing that needs cleansing. As a verb, it expresses the action of washing rather than the person or thing being washed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 52 times, with especially frequent use in Leviticus, where washing is repeatedly mentioned in instructions about cleansing. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding passage determines what is being washed and why.

This noun means “male prostitute”: a man involved in prostitution. It names a person rather than describing an action, quality, or general condition. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in Sirach 23:17. The word therefore has a specific personal reference, not a broad term for wrongdoing or sexual behavior in general. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “sold.” It describes something that has been sold or is offered in exchange for payment, functioning as a description rather than an action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the condition of being sold. gl: one who goes before to show the way; leader
d: one who goes before to show the way; leader

e.t: This word means “one who goes before to show the way; leader.” It describes a person who takes the lead, guiding others by going ahead of them. As a noun, it refers to the leader himself rather than to the act of leading. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:36. Its central idea is practical direction: someone moves ahead so that others may follow the right path.

This adverb means “freshly,” describing something as newly made, newly present, or recently occurring. It modifies an action or condition by pointing to its recentness rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times, in Deuteronomy, Ezekiel, and 2 Maccabees.
